{{Short description|Deceptive statement}}
{{Globalize|1=article|2=United States|date=June 2025}}
A '''half-truth''' is a [[deception|deceptive statement]] that includes some element of [[truth]]. The statement might be partly true, the statement may be [[Limited hangout|totally true, but only part of the whole truth]], or it may use some deceptive element, such as improper [[punctuation]], or [[double meaning]], especially if the intent is to deceive, [[Evasion (ethics)|evade]], [[blame]] or misrepresent the truth.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.m-w.com/dictionary/Half-truth |title=Merriam Webster Definition of Half-truth, August 1, 2007 |publisher=M-w.com |date=2012-08-31 |access-date=2013-10-02}}</ref>

==Purpose==
The purpose and/or consequence of a half-truth is to make something that is really only a [[belief]] appear to be [[knowledge]], or a truthful statement to represent the whole truth or possibly lead to a false conclusion. The order in which the true and false information is presented in a "half-truth" can make a difference in ultimate believability.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last1=Barchetti |first1=Alberto |last2=Neybert |first2=Emma |last3=Mantel |first3=Susan Powell |last4=Kardes |first4=Frank R. |title=The Half-Truth Effect and Its Implications for Sustainability |journal=Sustainability |date=2022 |volume=14 |issue=11 |page=6943 |doi=10.3390/su14116943 |publisher=MDPI |language=English|doi-access=free |bibcode=2022Sust...14.6943B }}</ref> Barchetti and colleagues show that when two unrelated statements are put together with syntax that suggests causality, the statement is believed if the premise is true (even if the conclusion is unrelated or false).  Conversely, if the false statement is placed in the premise, the combined statement is less likely to be believed. Thus the order of presentation can influence the credibility of a half-true statement and has been named the half-truth effect.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.mdpi.com/search?q=half+truth+effect&journal=sustainability&volume=14&issue=11 | title=MDPI – Publisher of Open Access Journals }}</ref>

==Examples==
* In January 2018, U.S. President [[Donald Trump]] claimed on Twitter that "because of my policies, Black Unemployment has just been reported to be at the LOWEST RATE EVER RECORDED!" Although the unemployment rate for black Americans was indeed at a record low, the rate had been consistently decreasing since 2010, seven years before Trump took office.<ref>{{cite web |last=Jacobson |first=Louis |date=January 31, 2018 |title=Donald Trump is partly correct in rejoinder to Jay-Z |url=http://www.politifact.com/truth-o-meter/statements/2018/jan/30/donald-trump/donald-trump-partly-correct-rejoinder-jay-z/ |website=Politifact}}</ref>
* Using a [[technicality]]: former U.S. President [[Bill Clinton]] famously engaged in a half-truth when he gave the testimony of "[[I did not have sexual relations with that woman, Ms. Lewinsky.]]" Here he engaged in an [[equivocation]] fallacy to deliberately indicate one particular meaning of the phrase "sexual relations", while intending another meaning, to deliberately mislead the court while still being able to later claim that "my statements were technically correct."{{Citation needed|date=April 2025}}
* Another example of using a technicality was U.S. President Trump's claim that taxes were being allocated for condoms to be sent to [[Gaza Strip]] during the [[Gaza war]], while the actual location was [[Gaza Province|Gaza Province, Mozambique]].<ref>{{Cite web |author=Al Jazeera Staff |title=Is the US sending $50m in condoms to Gaza as Trump claims? |url=https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/1/30/is-the-us-sending-50m-in-condoms-to-gaza-as-trump-claims |access-date=2025-03-22 |website=Al Jazeera |language=en}}</ref>
* The classic story about [[blind men and an elephant]]. Each blind man touches a different part of the elephant and reaches a different conclusion about the nature of the elephant; while each man's experience of the elephant is accurate, none of them have a full understanding of the nature of the beast. One may be touching the tail and believe that the elephant is long and thin; another may be touching the belly and say that it is round and big.{{Citation needed|date=April 2025}}

==Politics==
Some forms of half-truths are an inescapable part of politics in [[representative democracy|representative democracies]]. The reputation of a political candidate can be irreparably damaged if they are exposed in a lie, so a complex style of language has evolved to minimise the chance of this happening. If someone has not said something, they cannot reasonably be accused of lying. As a consequence, politics has become a world where half-truths are expected, and political statements are rarely accepted at face value.<ref name="htpolitics">{{cite book|title=The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the English Language|author=Crystal, David|author-link=David Crystal|year=2003|publisher=Cambridge University Press|page=378}}</ref>

[[William Safire]] defines a half-truth, for political purposes, as "a statement accurate enough to require an explanation; and the longer the explanation, the more likely a public reaction of half-belief".<ref>{{cite book|title=The New Language of Politics: An Anecdotal Dictionary of Catchwords, Slogans, and Political Usage|url=https://archive.org/details/newlanguageofpol00safi|url-access=registration|author=William Safire|author-link=William Safire|year=1968|publisher=[[Random House]]}}</ref>

It has been shown that the order of the half-truth makes a difference in reported belief in the statement. That is when a statement begins with a true statement followed by another unrelated statement (either true or false), the statement is believed. However, when the false statement is put in front, then the entire package is less believed regardless of whether the second part of the argument is true or false.<ref name=":0" /> This also indicates the [[anchoring effect]], which is a tendency of people to believe the first thing said which acts as an anchor point in believing, or disbelieving, what follows and is also found in reference pricing used in price promotions. Consumer behaviour and psychology studies show the heavy influence of the order and presentation of information in what beliefs people generally may be likely to form as well as decoy items that may be the early information.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Erta |first=Kristine |last2=Hunt |first2=Stefan |last3=Iscenko |first3=Zanna |last4=Brambley |first4=Will |date=April 2013 |title=Applying behavioural economics at the Financial Conduct Authority |url=https://www.fca.org.uk/publication/occasional-papers/occasional-paper-1.pdf |publisher=Financial Conduct Authority}}</ref>{{Reference page|pages=14-20}}<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/the-fallible-mind/201708/why-advertising-falls-flat-in-individuals-autism | title=Why Advertising Falls Flat in Individuals with Autism &#124; Psychology Today }}</ref>

In his 1990 work ''The Magic Lantern: The Revolution of 1989 Witnessed in Warsaw, Budapest, Berlin, and Prague'', [[Timothy Garton Ash]] responded to [[Václav Havel]]'s call for "living in truth":
{{cquote|Now we expect many things of politicians in a well-functioning parliamentary democracy. But "living in truth" is not one of them. In fact the essence of democratic politics might rather be described as "working in half-truth". Parliamentary democracy is, at its heart, a system of limited adversarial mendacity, in which each party attempts to present part of the truth as if it were the whole.<ref>{{cite book
|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=R1rRfwR-l8MC&q=havel+half.truth&pg=PA134
|title=The Revolutions of 1989
|author=Vladimir Tismaneanu
|year=1999
|publisher=Routledge
|isbn=0-415-16949-6}}</ref>}}

Philosopher [[Alfred North Whitehead]] was quoted as saying: "There are no whole truths; all truths are half-truths. It is trying to treat them as whole truths that play the devil".<ref>Alfred North Whitehead, ''Dialogues'', 1954: Prologue.</ref> If this is true, statements, or truths, which according to Whitehead are all half-truths, are susceptible to creating deceptive and false conclusions.

==Meme theory==
[[Richard Brodie (programmer)|Richard Brodie]] links half-truths to [[meme]]s, writing, "the truth of any proposition depends on the assumptions you make in considering it—the distinct memes you use in thinking about it".<ref name="brodie">{{cite book|title=Virus of the Mind: The New Science of the Meme|author=Brodie, Richard|year=1996|publisher=Integral Press, Seattle|page=51}}</ref> Brodie considers half-truths a necessary part of human interaction because they allow practical application of ideas when it is impractical to convey all the information needed to make a fully informed decision, although some half-truths can lead to false conclusions or [[inferences]] in the world of [[logic]].<ref name="brodie" />

==Quotations==
The notion of half-truths has existed in various cultures, giving rise to several [[epigram]]matic sayings.
* [[Karl Kraus (writer)|Karl Kraus]], an Austrian journalist, critic, playwright, and poet, noted, "An [[aphorism]] can never be the whole truth; it is either a half-truth or a truth-and-a-half."<ref>As quoted in [[Thomas Szasz]], ''Anti-Freud: Karl Kraus's Criticism of Psychoanalysis and Psychiatry'', 1990, p. 157.</ref>
* [[Arthur Koestler]], a Hungarian-British author and journalist, wrote, "Two half-truths do not make a truth, and two half-cultures do not make a culture."<ref>As quoted in [[Jonathon Green]], ''Says who?: a guide to the quotations of the century'', 1988, p. 451.</ref>

== Selective truth ==
{{See also|Selection bias}}
Selective truth is an act of telling some part of the truth selectively, both intentionally and unintentionally.<ref name="GillotCommSelectiveTruth" />

Both intentional and unintentional selective truth are not a truth at all.<ref name="bbcdeviousart">{{cite web|title=The devious art of lying by telling the truth|date=15 November 2017 |publisher=BBC|url=https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20171114-the-disturbing-art-of-lying-by-telling-the-truth|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230309164112/https://www.bbc.com/future/article/20171114-the-disturbing-art-of-lying-by-telling-the-truth|archive-date=2023-03-09|url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Ethics and morality ===
While selective truth information is not the truth information, whether telling selective truth is considered [[deceptive]] or [[lying]] and the morality are subject to debate. Some scholars think it is deceptive and lying and some scholars think the opposite. Some philosophers consider selective truth deceptive but not lying.<ref name="bbcdeviousart" /><ref name="missouritruth">{{cite web|title=TRUTH TELLING|publisher=Center of Health Ethics, School of Medicine, University of Missouri|url=https://medicine.missouri.edu/centers-institutes-labs/health-ethics/faq/truth-telling|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230310121646/https://medicine.missouri.edu/centers-institutes-labs/health-ethics/faq/truth-telling|archive-date=2023-03-10|url-status=live}}</ref> Some philosophers simply consider it not lying.<ref name="GillotCommSelectiveTruth">{{cite web |title=Selective Truth-Telling |url=https://www.gillottcommunications.com/selective-truth-telling/ |url-status= |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230316125718/https://www.gillottcommunications.com/selective-truth-telling/ |archive-date=2023-03-16 |publisher=Gillott Communication}}</ref>
